# simpleapp Call Adjacency Notes

`tests_disabled/live.py` was once treated as the place to look for simpleapp's entry point. The first thing to appear in the file is:

```python
from gevent.monkey import patch_all
patch_all()
```

This call is not wrapped in a visibly named function. When reading in module-load order, the patch happens first, and only then are the later tests and webagg imports processed. So when investigating a live scenario from this file, it's more reliable to note where gevent is loaded before guessing which object simpleapp belongs to.

The adjacent objects that appear next are limited to three:

```python
from pywb.webagg.test.testutils import LiveServerTests
from pywb.webagg.handlers import DefaultResourceHandler
from pywb.webagg.app import ResAggApp
```

They show that this page is not an isolated page sample. `LiveServerTests` puts the focus on the live server test side; `DefaultResourceHandler` is the resource-handling adjacency visible from the same file; and `ResAggApp` points the reading path toward the aggregate application. The file is located under `tests_disabled`, which also explains why this path is often reached through old links or historical tracing, but has not become a routine test entry point.

The initial notes described simpleapp as a “lightweight wrapper,” but that term is no longer precise. It implies that the wrapping happens in this file, while the visible content is only enough to confirm the import relationships and the module-level patch. ```text
live.py
  ├─ patch_all()                 runs first during module loading
  ├─ LiveServerTests             test-side entry
  ├─ DefaultResourceHandler      resource-handling neighbor
  └─ ResAggApp                   aggregate-application neighbor

An earlier note described this adjacency as “the test base class creates the application via the handler,” but that wording is no longer used; the file header provides no such direct call. `DOC-06` is a marginal note near toppest's implementation. The two pages may be opened together during the same pass through the old code, but this page does not explain toppest's behavior. # jquery-latest.min Callback Code Reading

`pywb/static/js/jquery-latest.min.js` is the sole entry point for this record. The callbacks are traced here within the file boundary; adjacent scripts or page-side logic are not brought in along the way. The filename contains `min`, so short variable names can only serve as clues to the current location and cannot be treated directly as stable interface names.

## How the Initial Draft Read It

The initial draft drew the relationship as a straight line:

```text
jquery-latest.min.js
        |
        v
   callback storage -> callback trigger -> failure/event exit
```

The working assumption at the time was: “The callback relationship can initially be understood as a one-way chain within the file; defer tracing the caller.” This statement is no longer suitable as a relationship conclusion, but it remains here. It shows that the initial code reading started inside the file, treated storage and triggering as two consecutive actions, and did not separately consider that the callback value might be passed on again.

The old diagram still has one use: it can help point the initial search in the right direction. It cannot prove that all callbacks are completed within the file, and it certainly cannot be used to name events, exceptions, or callers outside the file. The later review did not turn the old diagram into a new complete call graph; instead, it split it into several local locations to verify separately.

## Find the Value First, Then the Action

The first pass searches the minified source for places where the callback appears as a value. What needs to be recorded here is how it is created or stored: whether it is placed directly in an object, passed in as an argument, or temporarily held in an expression. Copying only the short variable name is not enough; the original snippet must retain at least enough surrounding context to show the assignment or argument-passing relationship.

The second pass follows the same value forward. If the callback continues to be passed as an argument, the passing point and the trigger point must be written separately; they may be adjacent in the minified file, or separated by another layer of expression. Do not treat “appeared once” as “has already executed,” and do not treat passing it to another object as meaning it has already left the file boundary.

The third pass looks for the actual call action. Confirm which local expression retrieves and triggers the callback, then split the trigger result into two categories: handling that remains inside the file, or a result that reaches an event exit or failure exit. The latter two are only the two directions to check back from on this page; seeing a branch does not justify filling in a specific event name or exception type.

```text
callback value appears
   |
   +-- stored or temporarily held
   |
   +-- passed on as a value
           |
           +-- retrieved and triggered somewhere in the file
           |       |
           |       +-- result returns to the file
           |       +-- result reaches an event exit
           |
           +-- leaves the file boundary (to be located)
```

“to be located” in the diagram describes a code-reading action, not a runtime conclusion. In particular, distinguish “the callback value leaves the file” from “the callback execution result leaves the file”: the former occurs through an argument or object relationship, while the latter occurs after triggering. If both are left as the same arrow, the caller is easily misrecorded as the trigger point later.

## Local Relationships to Record Within the File

| Code-reading location | What to record | What cannot be inferred directly |
|---|---|---|
| Creation or storage | What value the callback appears as, and whether it is placed in an object or argument | That the value has already executed |
| Continued passing | Which piece of file-local logic receives the value, and whether it can still be traced through the original context | That the receiving object is the final caller |
| Trigger action | Which local expression retrieves and calls it, and where the result goes | That all asynchronous paths belong to this file |
| Result branch | Whether the result returns to the file or reaches an event/failure exit | That an unnamed branch can be filled in as a common exception |

This table is the order for checking back through this file, not the dependency table for the entire replay page. Do not list common library names in the direct-dependency column yet; only add an object name when an object reference is visible in the actual snippet at `jquery-latest.min.js`. The page entry point, build artifacts, and other scripts cannot replace this condition.

## What Remains Unresolved After Review

What can be retained reliably at present is the file entry point, the JavaScript module classification in the index, and the four local locations of “storage—passing—trigger—exit.” Specific function names, event names, and failure types were not entered into this page’s review record, so they remain open items rather than being filled in with terminology from memory such as jQuery. The failure exit must be checked separately. The same applies to an event exit: record the event as a local relationship only when there is an explicit passing or triggering relationship within the file. Without this step, “failure/event exit” in the old diagram is only a search label.

“Understand it as a one-way chain within the file” was an old working assumption. It was later marked obsolete but not deleted. The adjacent document `DOC-08` records the callback relationship for `bootstrap.min`. Both pages are local readings of minified JavaScript; each file object must still be checked from its own entry point.

# History of service worker and media preservation

## Review at the entry point

The first version placed `pywb/rewrite/test/test_content_rewriter.py` too close to an implementation decision. The review started by returning to the test file itself: `BufferWARCWriter` and `GzippingWrapper` prepare the archive content, `StatusAndHeaders` allows the status and response headers to be set independently, `BytesIO` holds the byte content, and `CDXObject` provides the index object. This confirms how the samples are constructed, not where the service worker decision belongs.

These objects also changed the reading order. Looking only at the final page shows the result after the browser has continued processing; looking only at the status code does not tell us whether the content changed; finding a directory path alone does not explain where the browser's allowed scope comes from. The response body, response headers, and path relationships need separate records. The test file's name cannot be used to combine them into an implementation conclusion.

## Two directions in the old notes

The ordinary-resource approach had a practical appeal at the time: existing content processing seemed able to handle scripts, and callers could obtain an apparently convenient scope value from the directory of the replay URL. The other approach required identifying service worker responses first, then checking whether content and scope were each preserved. The former avoided a special branch; the latter required an additional object-type check.

Without samples, “the page opens” could only be a coarse observation. It did not show that the response body remained unchanged or that the returned scope covered the replayed origin. Leaving callers to fill in the scope was also just speculation, since there was no caller output available to review at the time.

## Back to the review

The review feedback did not make all scripts exceptions. It required separating three areas of observation: the response body before and after default content processing, the headers actually present in the response, and the relationship between the scope in the header and the replayed origin's path. This separation was intended to avoid treating one successfully opened page as three results.

A broader approach also came up in review: preserve ordinary HTML, service workers, media, srcset, and other embedded resources before processing them, routing them all through the same entry point. This approach was not adopted. The available material did not provide before-and-after processing results for each of these object types. If a difference appeared at a unified entry point, it would also be difficult to tell which type of object had changed the result.

## A limited attempt

The test setup could already prepare archived responses, byte content, and status and headers, so an attempt was made to separate content comparison from header comparison. First, save the input and inspect the content after default processing; then read the status and headers separately; finally, assess the scope alongside the replayed origin. The record had neither complete failure output nor enough caller-side page results, so the attempt was not recorded as verified to pass.

This attempt first withdrew the approximation that “the directory location of the replay URL is the scope.” The directory location can still help locate the page, but it does not automatically equal the replayed origin's root path. When the application is deployed outside the root directory, this distinction especially needs samples to illustrate it. There were no specific path or response header values at the time, so it could not be extended into a deployment compatibility conclusion.

## Adjacent items remain open

Listing media, srcset, and service workers together in the title only means they belong to the same round of compatibility closure work. Media and srcset need comparisons of attribute inputs and outputs; service workers need comparisons of the response body, response headers, and origin scope. A page showing no errors is not enough to draw conclusions for either kind of sample.

The old “scripts are just resources” statement remains in the record, with a note beside it identifying it as an early working assumption only. It once used path reuse and directory-based inference as reasons to expect only minor changes. Later review found that neither convenience was supported by observed results. The record therefore retains the candidates, review findings, and gaps rather than prematurely presenting a final rule.

# History of Service Worker and media Preservation

## 2023-04-19：A Note Tucked Beside the Test Entry Point

When this page was first left here, the scope to be finalized for R2026.09 was only a heading with two topics side by side：service worker response preservation and scope, and media and srcset preservation. The heading placed the two subjects together, but did not say that they shared an implementation. The work left to do at that point was to locate the relevant code, identify the objects involved, and add samples, rather than start by laying out a complete rule.

The path at hand was `pywb/rewrite/test/test_content_rewriter.py` under `internal/replay-core`, and the revision observed was `v_prev`. The following was visible at the top of the file：

```python
from warcio.warcwriter import BufferWARCWriter, GzippingWrapper
from warcio.statusandheaders import StatusAndHeaders
from io import BytesIO
from pywb.warcserver.index.cdxobject import CDXObject
```

These names made the test-side structure quite clear. `BufferWARCWriter` and `GzippingWrapper` could prepare archive content, `StatusAndHeaders` stored the status and headers, `BytesIO` received the bytes, and `CDXObject` gave the samples index objects. At the time, the note interpreted them as clues that “responses could be constructed and preserved”, but did not infer where service worker handling actually belonged from the import locations.

The first two candidate approaches were also written on the same page. The first was to treat service worker scripts as ordinary resources, process them through the content-rewriting path, and approximate the scope using the directory of the replay URL. The second was to treat them separately as a type of replay response, examining the content and the scope the browser could use separately. The first appeared to require fewer code changes, while the second acknowledged that the response body and the scope might be two different outcomes.

media and srcset were written in the lower half of the note. They had no samples, only a reminder：the fact that a page could still load in the end did not mean that the attribute values remained unchanged before and after processing. There was also no response-body comparison, header record, or result from the calling page for service workers. The initial draft stopped here, with neither direction decided on.

## Spring and Summer of 2023：A Misreading Caused by the Filename

When this path was reviewed later, the first interpretation to be corrected was that “the `content_rewriter` file is where the rules live”. A file could be a test-side construction entry point, or merely a navigation point to nearby code；its name could not substitute for implementation relationships. This correction did not remove the original path, because every subsequent discussion returned from this path to the response-construction objects.

`StatusAndHeaders` Make an old ambiguity obvious: response headers can be examined separately from the byte content. `BytesIO` It also reminds reviewers that the final page text is not the only result; the input response and the processed response body can be saved as two separate things. Seeing only that the page is still displayed cannot determine whether content processing changed the response; seeing only the status code cannot determine whether the range received by the browser is appropriate.

At this point, the discussion is split into three aspects. The first is the response body before and after default content processing. The second is the status and headers actually returned. The third is whether the range expressed by the headers should be compared with the root path of the replayed origin, rather than directly equated with the ordinary directory containing the page or the application's mount location. This split is still a review method, not a call chain tied to a particular function.

The review margin note also left a classification reminder: do not mix page text, ordinary embedded resources, and service workers into one type of object just because a resource looks like a script. It gives neither a function name nor a production command, so here we retain only the fact that it changed the direction of the analysis. The response body and range of service workers are considered separately, while media and srcset continue to await attribute-level samples.

## 2023-10-06: The old approach remains in place

> Old approach: the service worker script first follows the ordinary content rewrite path; if the page can load, infer the scope from the directory containing replay URL; the caller fills in the headers.

This section was later marked “deprecated” but was not deleted. It explains why the early approach favored the ordinary resource path: the existing entry point appeared able to handle scripts, and the directory could provide an easy-to-use approximate scope. Without response-header samples, an approximation can easily be treated as fact.

There is no production failure record to cite for this old approach. It was overturned because of object confusion, not because of a complete incident log. Whether the content was changed must be determined from the response body; how large a range the browser can use must be determined from the actual headers and their relationship to the replayed origin. The page not reporting an immediate error only indicates that this page flow did not stop at a visible error; it cannot answer both questions at once.

“Fill in the headers through the caller” was also returned to the unconfirmed category. The existing file entry point can prepare samples, but there are no caller-provided header values, page return, or registration result. Writing this sentence as an operational step would disguise a guess as an interface action that has already occurred, so it is preserved only as part of the old approach.

The review also proposed a larger unified entry point: ordinary HTML, service workers, media, srcset, and other embedded resources would be retained first and then processed further from the same place. This direction appeared capable of reducing scattered decisions, but there were no before-and-after comparisons for the different types of objects at the time. If a unified entry point produces a difference, the existing material cannot determine which type of object changed, nor can it prove that this approach is more reliable than narrow-scope processing, so it was not selected.

## An unfinished sample check

A targeted check was performed during review, with the goal of separating the response content and response headers from the same page result. The archive write object, byte buffer, and status-and-header object were all visible on the test side, so the check sequence was changed to first prepare the input response, then compare the response body before and after default processing, then read the status and headers, and finally examine the scope alongside the origin being replayed.

This check did not leave a complete output. There was no consistent failure text, nor a set of caller results that could establish the scope after registration in the browser. The record therefore did not say “passed” or “fix complete,” but instead retained the changes to the sample structure: content comparisons cannot be replaced with the page's final text, header comparisons cannot be replaced with a mere existence check, and origin scope cannot be inferred directly from the directory name.

The first claim withdrawn during the attempt was that “the directory location is the scope.” The directory for replaying URL is still useful for locating the page, but it does not inherently carry the semantics of the root path of the origin being replayed. When an application is located in a non-root directory, the page path, mount location, and origin root path may each play different roles. The current materials do not contain a set of actual inputs, response headers, and page results for a non-root path, so this remains a boundary issue rather than being written up as coverage of a particular deployment setup.

Another unresolved point is what specific test result should substantiate “no content rewriting occurred.” The review had already distinguished this result from page text, but at the time there was no fixed field name, test function name, or assertion output. The document retains only this observation requirement and does not invent a nonexistent API name for the test file.

## Side notes on media and srcset

media and srcset appeared alongside service workers from the outset, but were still not incorporated into the service worker decision later. They are page attributes, and the evidence they require is their values before and after attribute processing; the service worker dispute, by contrast, centers on the content and scope of specific replay responses. Calling both groups “resource preservation” can actually obscure the differences.

An overly broad criterion was proposed early on: if the page could continue loading, media and srcset could be considered preserved. This criterion was later crossed out, but remains in the historical account. It came from an attempt to quickly narrow the surface area for compatibility closure, not from the results of an attribute comparison sample. A page might not use a particular attribute, or rewriting an attribute might temporarily have no effect on rendering; neither case demonstrates that the value was preserved.

Therefore, subsequent materials for media and srcset need to retain the input attributes and processing results separately. The scope header on a service worker response cannot indirectly prove that the two attributes were preserved; page results for media and srcset likewise cannot prove that a service worker response body was not processed. These adjacent issues remain in the history because they explain why the title has continued to list them together, not because the current decision covers them.

## 2023-10-09: The sequence left by returning to the page during review

The post-review record did not simply replace the old direction with the opposite conclusion. It first documented the observation sequence, then the object boundaries. First, preserve the input response and compare the content before and after processing; next, read the status and response headers independently; finally, compare the scope with the replayed origin path. This sequence is intended to prevent the final page, status code, or directory location from prematurely standing in for the actual object under examination.

The meeting excerpts also included a practical concern: if ordinary HTML, service workers, and other embedded resources all go through the same “preserve first, process later” entry point, object-level fault localization will be lost when a failure occurs. This concern was not a comprehensive performance assessment of a unified entry point; it only indicated that the existing samples were insufficient to support a cross-object change in one go. The unified entry point was therefore archived as an option not adopted, while the narrow-scope decision was kept separate for now.

The same page also retained two unanswered questions. First, whether there is already an independent sample of the origin root path obtained from the service worker response in a non-root-path deployment. Second, which test interface will ultimately carry the observed value reporting “no content rewriting occurred.” The former lacks path values and response header values; the latter lacks fixed fields and assertion output. Neither was rewritten as completed work.

## 2025-09-02: Current position appended later

After retaining the old proposal, local sample checks, the media and srcset side branches, and the review sequence, the current decision narrows the scope to service worker replay. The current position is recorded verbatim as follows: when DefaultRewriter handles sw_ service worker replay, it must bypass content URL rewriting, directly preserve the original response body, and report that no content rewriting occurred, while also setting the Service-Worker-Allowed header on the response with the replayed origin root path as its scope.

The two outcomes in this statement still need to be considered separately. Preserving the original response body answers whether this type of replay object enters content URL rewriting; setting `Service-Worker-Allowed` answers whether the allowed scope received by the browser is based on the replayed origin root path. One outcome cannot substantiate the other, and an ordinary resource directory cannot supply these two values from the sidelines either.

The current position refers only to the object boundaries when DefaultRewriter handles `sw_` service worker replay. It does not turn ordinary HTML, ordinary page scripts, media, srcset, or other embedded resources into unprocessed responses, nor does it claim that all mounting methods have been validated. The special response rules for service workers and page attribute preservation remain two adjacent but independent areas of finalization.

`StatusAndHeaders` and `BytesIO` in the test file are still suitable entry points for verification: one helps inspect response headers separately, while the other helps preserve response bytes.`BufferWARCWriter`, `GzippingWrapper`, and `CDXObject` are still local navigation terms when preparing samples for archiving. They support reading how to construct samples, but are insufficient on their own to prove the implementation call relationship; the trace-back still starts from the local entry point `pywb/rewrite/test/test_content_rewriter.py`.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> InitialNote
    state "Initial parallel notes" as InitialNote
    state "Standard resource assumption" as OrdinaryResource
    state "Observe response body and range separately" as SplitObservation
    state "Narrow boundary of the service worker" as NarrowBoundary
    state "media and srcset pending completion" as MediaSrcsetOpen
    InitialNote --> OrdinaryResource
    OrdinaryResource --> SplitObservation
    SplitObservation --> NarrowBoundary
    SplitObservation --> MediaSrcsetOpen
    NarrowBoundary --> [*]
```

## Boundaries Still Open After the Current Position

Deployment under a non-root path was not incidentally validated by the current decision. The decision has already scoped this to the root path of the origin being replayed, but the materials do not provide the complete paths, response headers, and page results when the application is mounted under a non-root directory. This gap cannot be used to support the old directory inference in reverse, nor can it be written up as deployment compatibility having been closed out.

media and srcset still require attribute-level comparison. If only the final page state remains later, first confirm whether the pre-processing attributes, post-processing attributes, and actual page paths using those attributes are available. Without these objects, the page continuing to display can only be treated as a coarse-grained phenomenon, insufficient to draw conclusions about either attribute.

The location that holds the “no content rewriting occurred” result has not yet been given a fixed name in the existing materials either. The current document does not add fields, does not treat `StatusAndHeaders` as a content comparison result, and does not treat `BytesIO` as a scope determination result. Each of the three sets of materials has a limited use; if explicit test output becomes available later, the observed values can then be matched to the actual interfaces.

## Old Examples Kept in the Appendix

### Example One: Choosing the Path by Resource Name

The old note used “script” as the sole classification criterion, assuming that any object that looked like a script could follow the ordinary content rewriting path. It did not save the response headers or record the root path of the origin being replayed. This example is outdated, but keeping it illustrates why resource names cannot replace determining what kind of object is being replayed.

### Example Two: Treating a Page Opening as Attribute Preservation

Another old example put media, srcset, and service workers into the “page can open” result cell. It did not record attribute inputs, attribute outputs, or service worker response headers. This example was later explicitly overturned: the page-level result is too coarse to demonstrate attribute preservation or that the scope comes from the correct source.

### Example Three: Using Directory Location in Place of Scope

An early draft inferred the scope a service worker could cover from the directory of the replayed URL. It had no non-root-path samples and no caller-side header results. This approach is no longer applicable; the directory can help locate the page, but cannot by itself prove the origin scope allowed by the browser.

### Example Four: Preserving All Objects First Through a Unified Approach

A unified-entry-point proposal raised during review envisioned ordinary HTML, service workers, media, srcset, and other embedded resources following the same processing approach. It was not adopted, not because a complete failure report already existed, but because the current comparison materials were insufficient to determine whether different objects could share this boundary. This proposal remains in the history as an option that was not adopted.

These old examples leave behind four clues that were once relied upon: resource names, page results, directory locations, and a unified entry point. They all help explain the early assessments, but none can replace the observations of response bodies, response headers, and replayed origin paths that are currently needed.

# Capture Fallback and Non-Root Deployment Plan

First, one easily confused scenario: the resource capture returns 3xx, while Location points back to the target currently being replayed. The old idea was to treat it as an ordinary redirect and hand it directly to the client; that is the simplest option, but if the www host and its corresponding bare host point back to each other, the client will keep looping.

There are two candidate approaches:

- Return 3xx unchanged. This requires little change, but leaves the problem with the caller.
- Detect redirects that point back to the current target, discard that capture, and continue looking for the previously usable capture.

I lean toward the second option, but the comparison scope for the “current target” is not yet defined. With a non-root path deployment, the replay URL has an additional mount prefix, so we cannot compare only the bare paths; this needs to be reviewed in the same pass as fallback selection. Otherwise, a normal cross-path redirect could be misclassified as a self-redirect.

Start by tracing back from `pywb/warcserver/resource/responseloader.py` to the resource-loading entry point, then compare one self-redirect sample with one ordinary 3xx sample. If the capture found by fallback does not match the original target, withdraw this branch first rather than expanding it to all redirects.

# Capture Fallback and Non-Root Deployment Plan

The previous version placed “return 3xx” alongside “continue looking for a capture.” After the actual review, we need to distinguish the two types of objects first: the redirect itself is a response in the archive, while the replay target is the address already resolved for the current request. Fallback should intervene only when both point to the same replay target; capture cannot be skipped just because the status code is 3xx.

### Candidate path after review

1. Read Location from the capture and resolve it in the current replay context.
2. Compare it with the current request target. Preserve host differences during comparison, especially the loop from the www host to the corresponding bare host.
3. After detecting a self-redirect, continue using the previously available capture; expose the original failure result only when no usable capture is available.

This keeps ordinary external redirects on the existing processing path and avoids using an “always fallback” switch to mask a missing capture. The tradeoff is that we need to confirm how “previously available” is propagated: if it is saved only temporarily in the current function, the mount prefix for a non-root-path deployment may be lost during the next parse; if the complete replay address is passed down, we also need to check whether existing callers depend on the old path format.

The confirmed entry point for review remains `pywb/warcserver/resource/responseloader.py`. The time-conversion function in the file header and `to_native_str` are direct dependencies, but they cannot by themselves establish ownership of the fallback. RPL-202 retain coverage items for self-redirect capture fallback, while RPL-219 retain abnormal-state cases after non-root-path deployment. Both cards are only sample entry points; unconfirmed implementation details should not be written as conclusions.

### Still undecided

- Whether host normalization occurs before comparison or after capture selection.
- Which layer stores the mount prefix.
- When there is no previous capture, whether to return 3xx unchanged or record the result as non-fallbackable.

Do not submit a cross-layer refactor until sample results are available for all three points.

# Capture Fallback and Non-Root Deployment Proposal

The earliest draft framed the issue as “whether to pass 3xx through.” That framing was too broad: the same class of status codes includes both responses where the archived page genuinely requires a client redirect and captures that send the request back to itself. Fallback logic must not swallow the former; only the latter warrants looking for an older capture. Another point of disagreement left over from review was non-root deployment. When a page is mounted under an application prefix, the address used for comparison, the address passed to the next layer, and the address ultimately returned to the caller may not be the same string.

### Proposal to Retain for Now

Make fallback a branch in resource selection rather than rewriting all 3xx:

- First, get Location from the capture response, then resolve it against the replay request. Relative addresses cannot be compared in isolation from the mount prefix.
- Compare the resolved result with the replay target. The host cannot simply be stripped out; the comparison needs to cover loops from a www host to its corresponding bare host while retaining the effects of the port, path, and query string.
- If a self-redirect is detected, do not treat this 3xx as the final resource. Continue resolving a usable capture already found earlier; if no usable capture was found earlier, follow the original handling path for cases with no fallback candidate.
- If no self-redirect is detected, leave the normal redirect path unchanged. This prevents the added check from turning an external redirect into a static resource or page content.

When resource loading encounters a 3xx capture that points back to the replay target of the request, it must not return that redirect as the terminal result. It must identify the self-redirect and continue resolving a previously available capture, including loops from a www host to its corresponding bare host.

“Previously available” does not mean any preceding record. It must still correspond to the resource requested; otherwise, fallback merely hides the capture error behind different content. One implementation option is to carry the preceding capture through the resource-loading call stack. Another is to have the selection layer return “candidates already checked.” The two approaches have different costs. The former has a smaller change footprint, but we need to confirm that the non-root path prefix is not stripped during recursion or another resolution pass. The latter makes the state easier to express, but may affect the return shape existing callers expect. These are proposals only; neither is being recorded as a decided interface.

### Counterexamples and Stopping Points

The first counterexample is a normal 302 pointing to an off-site address. It does not point back to the target, so the status code alone must not trigger fallback. The second is a deployment combination where the target lacks the prefix but Location includes it; if the two are normalized at different layers, different strings do not necessarily mean different resources. The third is redirects back and forth between www and bare hosts; comparing only the full URL without specifying how the hosts correspond will still miss the loop.

Start the review at `pywb/warcserver/resource/responseloader.py`. This file is a starting point for inspecting resource-loading behavior; its location alone cannot determine all cross-layer relationships. RPL-202 covers fallback from self-redirecting captures, while RPL-219 covers abnormal state after non-root deployment. The former should provide fallback samples, and the latter should provide mount-prefix scenarios. Examine the two sets of samples independently; success in one must not be used to cover the other type of path.

### Rollback Conditions

If the capture selected by fallback cannot be shown to still correspond to the requested resource, stop at the original failure result rather than expanding the candidate range. If the prefix is lost in a non-root path scenario, first roll back the cross-layer passing changes and retain only normal redirect behavior. If determining the relationship between www and bare hosts requires going beyond the resource-selection layer, leave that item unresolved rather than inventing a new normalization entry point in this proposal.

The storage location for candidate captures, the specific layer that determines host correspondence, and the final presentation of the original 3xx when there is no candidate remain undecided. These three points should be decided using both implementation snippets and caller-visible results.

# Trailing Slash and Multibyte Decoding Troubleshooting Tree

## Symptoms

For the same capture URL, one request enters replay, while another that differs only in the `/` at the end of its path gets redirected or cannot find a capture record. First copy the request URL, the matched capture URL, and the query string; do not overwrite the original value with a concatenated string first.

Another case involves reading the response in chunks. English content is usually fine; when a multibyte character is split across two chunks, the output may contain a replacement character, or the later chunk may be treated as the start of a new character. First confirm whether the anomaly is in reading, decoding, or output; do not collapse all three layers into a single encoding error.

## Previous Triage

- If the capture URL has a trailing slash and the request does not, first check the URL matching branch and redirect target; record the query component separately.
- If the trailing slashes match on both sides, check whether the capture conditions and query strings differ.
- If garbled output occurs only during chunked reads, save the raw chunk boundaries and compare them with the complete response.
- If the complete response is also incorrect, check character-set detection; if the complete response is correct but the chunked response is not, do not yet classify it as a URL issue.

Without the original request, capture URL, and chunk boundaries, record only the symptoms. `pywb/rewrite/test/test_wburl.py` is the follow-up location indicated by the old troubleshooting record; production routing or decoder ownership cannot be determined from the filename alone.

An early note described the missing trailing slash as an ordinary directory-concatenation difference and recommended adding the slash before rebuilding the query string. It did not say whether the query string was preserved verbatim, so leave that as a working hypothesis.

At the time, the multibyte issue was handled by decoding each chunk independently. The English sample did not expose the problem; it has not been confirmed whether the read layer retained incomplete bytes from the previous chunk, or whether the test helper code changed the chunk boundaries.

The review only required the request URL, capture URL, and response content to be preserved separately; the specific implementation entry point has not been decided.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Trailing Slashes and Multibyte Decoding

## Review entry

This page originally grouped two phenomena that often appear together: a trailing slash affects path capture matching, while response chunking affects text decoding. During review, save the request URL, the matched capture URL, the query string, the raw response chunks, and the final text separately. If all you have is the address ultimately displayed by the browser, you cannot determine whether an intermediate redirect changed the query portion.

The old record still points to `pywb/rewrite/test/test_wburl.py`. This path provides a test-side lookup entry; the path name alone cannot prove that the production route or decoder is here. Check actual references against the revision associated with the record.

## Path branch

When there is a capture but the request did not enter replay as expected, first put the path and query string in separate columns.

1. Compare the trailing portions of the path in capture URL and request URL; do not include the query string in the path comparison.
2. If the only difference is a trailing slash, record the response status and the complete value of `Location`.
3. Compare the query string in `Location` with the original request. If parameters disappeared, the order changed, or the string was re-encoded, stop at the URL normalization branch.
4. If the trailing portions match, investigate the capture-matching conditions; do not continue inferring on this page.

An old note still says, “Add the slash first, then rebuild the query string.” After review, it cannot be used as the default fix because there is no evidence that rebuilding it preserves the original value. Here, only require the complete `Location` to be retained; do not treat the page eventually opening as a pass.

If you can see only the second request, first record that the first hop is missing; if you can see only the address bar, it cannot substitute for the first-hop target. Mark path differences and query differences separately, or the next review will still combine the two changes. If the first-hop target and the original request appear identical, save the original string as well; do not keep only the normalized result displayed by the browser.

## Chunking branch

When replacement characters appear, split the input into the complete raw response, raw chunks saved at their actual boundaries, the intermediate decoded result, and the final output. Compare them in this order:

- If the complete response can be reconstructed but the chunked result cannot, check whether incomplete bytes were carried across chunk boundaries.
- If the complete response is already abnormal, inspect the content source and character-set declaration first; do not put the blame on the chunking logic.
- If the raw chunks are identical but the intermediate results differ, retain the decoded value before output and trace back along the conversion points.
- If there are no actual chunk boundaries, stop at the lack of evidence; do not guess that it is a cross-chunk issue from the shape of the garbled text.

There is one counterexample from the review: an entire block of English split into many chunks still decodes correctly. This sample only shows that it does not cover a multibyte boundary; splitting a multibyte character between adjacent chunks is what may expose boundary handling. If the rewrite layer has already changed the text, also save the decoded result before rewriting; do not infer the decoder input from the final HTML.

This review did not confirm whether the decoder received raw chunks or already-concatenated content, and it did not confirm whether the test helper copied, merged, or re-split the chunks. If the helper input does not have the same boundaries as the input actually read, the test result can only be recorded as an observation and cannot directly replace the production material.

## Review addendum

The review comment required “path differences” and “text differences” to be separated, but did not require connecting them into one end-to-end flow. This version therefore keeps two branches. The path branch needs the request, the capture object, and the first-hop target; the encoding branch needs the raw bytes, chunk boundaries, and intermediate text.

Unconfirmed items:

- The comparison value actually used to match URL;
- Whether normalization occurs before the redirect or when the target is generated;
- Whether the decoder receives raw chunks or already-concatenated content;
- Whether the incomplete bytes from the previous chunk are still present in the intermediate value when the failure occurs;
- Whether the chunk boundaries saved on the test side are the same as those at the read site.

## Field notes

Do not use the garbled text displayed on the page in place of the raw response, and do not screenshot only the final address. If you can obtain only one of them, explicitly record which one is missing. Once the address bar is already showing the second state, store it separately from the first-hop response. `pywb/rewrite/test/test_wburl.py` is still an available lookup location, but this page does not extend the file location into a production call chain.

This version still does not decide whether the query string is passed through unchanged by the routing layer, nor which layer should retain cross-chunk state. Keep both questions in their respective branches; do not cover them with the same “normalization” or “encoding” label.

# Trailing Slash and Multibyte Decoding Troubleshooting Tree

## Old Note by the Entry Point

When this page was first written, there was only one easily confused symptom on hand: requests appeared to point to the same capture object, but whether the path ended with a slash caused different results in the browser. The early note described this as a directory concatenation issue and suggested adding the slash first, then appending the parameters again. The original wording is preserved because several later investigations did indeed follow the string concatenation approach.

There were few actions available at the time: copy the request URL; copy the matched capture URL; check whether the response was a redirect; put the query string on a separate line. If only the URL ultimately displayed in the browser was kept, there was no way to see what the first hop had done. The initial record did not provide the matching function, nor did it connect the test-side path to the production entry point.

This old note also treated “the page eventually opens” as the result. It did not distinguish between the first-hop response, subsequent requests, and the page the browser already held, so it can only serve as background from the incident, not as standalone evidence that path handling was correct.

## 2023-03 On-Call Margin Notes

A narrower guideline was added during on-call duty: if the path ending differs, look at the path first; if the query parameters differ, open a separate item. Do not repeatedly call “normalization” on the same string, or it will be impossible to tell whether the change comes from the slash or the parameters.

The tree at the time was as follows:

```text
A capture exists, but replay is not entered as expected?
├─ Only the path ending differs?
│  ├─ Yes: copy the redirect status and the full target URL
│  └─ No: go to the capture matching records
└─ Replacement characters appear in the content?
   ├─ Only with chunked input: save the chunk boundaries
   └─ Also in the complete response: check the charset and raw content first
```

The stopping points for that shift were: without the complete request, matched URL, and returned target, do not infer path rules from what appears on the page; without the original chunk boundaries, do not describe “cross-chunk” behavior as a proven cause either. At that point, this was only an on-call troubleshooting procedure, not an implementation-level decision.

The on-call record did not preserve the request method or all headers from the first-hop response. Later, someone continued the investigation by posting only the final URL, making it impossible to determine whether the query string changed on the first hop or in a subsequent request. This gap belongs to the recording practices at the time and should not be filled in with invented details after the fact.

## Old Conclusion, Preserved but Deprecated

> When the trailing slash is missing, add it first, then reconstruct the query string; this should return to the same capture object.

This passage was an early working hypothesis. It did not specify whether reconstructing the query string preserved the query values verbatim, nor did it require saving the first-hop `Location`, so it could not later be used directly as operational guidance. The old passage is not rewritten into a correct version, to avoid erasing what was unknown at the time.

There was also a broader judgment at the time: if the page eventually opened, this difference could be classified as directory entry-point behavior. That judgment also lacked records of intermediate responses, so it could not distinguish between a successful redirect, a successful second request, or the browser retrieving the page from cache. It remains here as part of the old incident context, not as a stopping condition.

This old conclusion once treated the path and query string as a single piece of text to concatenate. A later review found that, at least in the records, the two must be separated; otherwise, even if the page was visible after the redirect, there was no way to answer whether the parameters retained their original values. This correction to the records is not extended here into a rule for all URL.

## 2023-10: A failed attempt at chunk-by-chunk decoding

During the second cleanup pass, someone had multibyte responses decoded immediately as each chunk arrived, on the grounds that each chunk could then be passed to the rewriter as soon as possible. The English sample passed, and single-byte characters did not expose any problems either; after a multibyte character was split across two adjacent chunks, replacement characters appeared in the output. This result disproved the assumption that “chunk boundaries do not matter,” but did not establish which layer had dropped the incomplete bytes.

The verification procedure was therefore changed to save three sets of source material and one result: the complete raw response, the raw chunks actually read, the decoded intermediate values, and the rewritten output. When the complete response can be recovered but the chunk-by-chunk result cannot, first check whether incomplete bytes are carried over between chunks; when neither can be recovered, first check the content itself and the charset declaration; when identical inputs produce different intermediate results, trace the transformation points before output.

One easily misleading successful sample was an entire English passage split into many chunks, with completely normal results. It only showed that this sample had not split any characters, and could not be used to close the multibyte-boundary branch. Conversely, seeing only replacement characters on the final page does not prove that the read layer is where bytes were lost.

This failure also left behind an operational distinction. If the chunks are merged first and only the merged string is saved, it becomes impossible to reconstruct which two chunks a character had spanned. Troubleshooting records therefore need to preserve the actual boundaries; if test helper code has already reorganized the input, that change must be marked separately, rather than treating the helper input as the raw network input.

At the time, it was not confirmed whether the error occurred during reading, concatenation, decoding, or rewriting. Someone initially recorded it as “a reader problem,” but that claim came only from the sequence of observed symptoms, with no code snippets or intermediate values to support it. Later records retained this attribution as a trace of the failed attempt, rather than turning it into a definitive conclusion.

## The ordering dispute left by the review

The review addendum asked that URL and decoding not be presented as a straight line of “normalize first, then output.” Both may manifest on the same page, but they require different evidence: path issues require the request, the captured object, and the redirect target; decoding issues require the raw bytes, chunk boundaries, and intermediate text.

The review also asked that the old explanation be retained so readers could see why troubleshooting had, for a time, focused on reassembling the query string. This request provided no new implementation details, so this page only changes the order of the records and does not expand the review comments into claims about production behavior.

Another ordering question came up during the review: if an address redirect and garbled text occur at the same time, should the path be handled first, followed by the content? The final opinion retained was not a fixed order, but a requirement to save the two sets of evidence separately. The address branch depends on the first hop, while the decoding branch depends on the raw chunks; if either set of material is missing, stop only at the corresponding branch.

Another assessment retained was that `pywb/rewrite/test/test_wburl.py` is only the source-code path pointed to by the old troubleshooting records. It can serve as an entry point for tracing back, but the filename alone cannot determine where the implementation resides. References corresponding to the path still need to be confirmed within `v_prev`; this page did not infer the entire project's call chain from a single test file.

## Side items left from around the year 2024

Between several reviews, one question about the test input remains open: whether the URL string used by the test helper code is the same value compared on the routing side. The existing records contain only the test path and issue name, which is not enough to connect the two. The test can reproduce the result produced by an input, but the production entry point's use of the same comparison value cannot be inferred from the file location.

Another adjacent item is whether blocks are merged before entering the decoder. If the read layer has already merged them, the result of manually chunking them in the test cannot directly describe what happens in the field; if not, whether the incomplete bytes from the previous block remain in state still requires intermediate values. No owner replied on this issue at the time, and there was no new output fragment, so it remains blank.

Another nearby record notes that if the rewrite layer changes the text after decoding, the pre-rewrite value must also be saved. The final page may already contain other rewrites, so the content received by the decoder cannot be inferred from it. This does not mutually prove anything with the trailing-slash branch; it is included here because the two symptoms once appeared on the same page.

## Field correction for 2025-03

Following the most recent field feedback, the trailing-slash branch no longer treats the query string as an auxiliary field that needs to be regenerated. During troubleshooting, save the request target, matched capture URL, and redirect target side by side exactly as they are. If the target has already been redirected, first check the status code and `Location`, then check whether the page makes another request; do not use the address after refresh in place of the first hop.

The current guidance is: when the matched capture URL ends with a slash but the request URL lacks a trailing slash, the replay route returns 307 to the address with the slash added, while preserving the query string exactly as-is, for example /?foo=bar.

This guidance is placed after the historical branch so users can see which part of the old approach it replaces. It handles only this boundary between the matched capture URL and the request URL; if no capture object was matched, the path itself is different, or the query value needs to be re-encoded, return to the corresponding branch instead and do not apply the status code here.

The current guidance changes the confirmed replay-route behavior, not the comparison method for all similar strings. In the field, still save the request, matched capture URL, first-hop status, and complete target. If any one of these four items is missing, the record can describe the observed symptom, but the first hop cannot be reconstructed from the final address.

## How to work through the address branch in the field

First save the request method, request URL, matched capture URL, and the status and target of the first-hop response. Here, the complete address includes the query string; do not copy only the path. If the record comes from a browser, note whether it is the first-hop network response or the final address bar; they are not the same evidence.

```text
Request not entering replay for the captured object?
├─ Captured URL has a trailing slash; requested URL does not
│  ├─ First-hop response available: check the status and full Location
│  └─ No first-hop response: stop at missing redirect evidence
├─ Both have matching endings
│  └─ Switch to the capture-matching or response branch
└─ The paths themselves also differ
   └─ Do not apply the trailing-slash branch; retain both URL
```

If the target has an added slash but its query string differs from the original request, stop at the redirect branch, retain both addresses, and wait for confirmation from the URL side. Do not re-encode the parameters before comparing them, as this would overwrite the original differences. If only the second request is available, record that the first hop is missing; if all you can see is that the page opens, you still cannot infer that the first-hop target was correct.

If both have matching endings but the page still does not enter the expected replay, do not continue investigating slashes just because of this page terminology. Record the capture-matching conditions as a separate item. If the request method or the resource requested by the second request changes, save each separately as well; do not write the results of subsequent requests back into the first hop.

Even if the first-hop target appears to have only one extra path character, retain the status and target in their original forms. Do not copy a slash automatically added by the address bar back into the request URL, and do not treat subsequent resource requests as the original page request. Record differences in the paths themselves, their endings, and their query strings separately; if one item is unconfirmed, the other two can still be checked first.

## On-site troubleshooting for the decoding branch

Do not change the charset declaration first. First determine which layer shows the anomaly: whether the raw bytes have already changed, chunk concatenation has changed the decoding input, replacement characters appear in an intermediate decoding value, or changes appear only in the rewritten text. At each layer, record only the values actually observed; do not substitute the final HTML for intermediate results.

```text
Does the output contain replacement characters?
├─ The complete raw response is already abnormal
│  └─ Save the charset declaration and switch to checking the content source
├─ The complete response is normal, but the chunked result is abnormal
│  ├─ Actual chunk boundaries available: compare the bytes on both sides of each boundary
│  └─ No chunk boundaries available: stop at insufficient evidence
├─ Raw input is identical, but intermediate decoding results differ
│  └─ Retain both intermediate values and trace back through the conversion points
└─ Only the rewritten text is abnormal
   └─ Save the text before rewriting first; do not attribute this to the read layer
```

A cross-chunk sample must at least specify which two chunks the character is split between. Merely writing “garbled Chinese text” or “intermittent encoding error” is not enough, because neither description distinguishes input corruption from boundary handling. A complete verification record should be able to answer: what the complete response is, how the actual chunks are split, which part the decoder receives first, and in which intermediate value the replacement character first appears.

If the full response can be restored but the chunked result cannot, first check whether incomplete bytes are being carried between chunks. If the full response itself cannot be restored, first inspect the raw content and charset declaration. If the raw chunks obtained by the two reading methods are completely identical but the results differ, trace the conversion points before output. When there are no actual chunk boundaries, record at most “Unable to distinguish whole-buffer decoding from cross-chunk processing”; do not add a cause.

If the replay layer also rewrites the content, save the decoding result before rewriting before the final page. The final page may already contain other rewrites, so it cannot be used to infer which bytes the reading layer received. If garbling appears only after following a redirect, retain the responses for both requests; without a second response, record only that they occurred simultaneously, not a causal relationship.

## Both branches occur simultaneously

The same page may both redirect and contain replacement characters. The processing order is not a fixed “fix the address first, then fix the encoding”; instead, first save the first-hop response and the first raw content separately. The address branch looks only at the request, capture, and `Location`; the encoding branch looks only at the raw bytes, chunk boundaries, and intermediate text.

If the first hop returns the target address and garbling appears only on the second request, first distinguish whether the resource changed and whether the reading method changed, then compare the two responses. If the responses from the two requests differ, the text problem in the second request cannot be used to explain the path behavior of the first hop. If the same raw response behaves differently under full and chunked reads, first complete the chunking evidence; do not attribute the multibyte issue to the trailing slash just because the URL phenomenon is also present.

The reverse also applies: an abnormal redirect target cannot be proven by a garbled sample. Only when the first-hop status, target address, complete raw response, chunk boundaries, and intermediate text have all been retained can the two branches be placed in the same incident record. If any one set is missing, register the gap separately; do not combine the two unknowns into a single conclusion.

If the two anomalies come from two different requests, split them by request first; if they come from the same response, split them by stage first. Do not fill the address branch's result into the decoding branch just to make the tree look complete, and do not treat the decoder's replacement characters as evidence that the query string was rewritten. The purpose here is simply to prevent one incident record from covering another.

## Excerpt from an old meeting

At one meeting, someone said: “First separate the slash and parameters and examine them; don't use the final page as evidence.” This is suitable for explaining why URL was required to be saved side by side at the time, but it did not provide an implementation decision or require all replay requests to follow the same branch.

Another discussion called chunked decoding “the reader's problem.” This was only the attribution at the time, and was later weakened by cross-chunk samples: the samples showed that boundary handling needed to be checked, but did not localize the issue to the reader itself. The original attribution is retained here and is not the current conclusion.

The review also raised a practical question: if the first hop `Location` is no longer in the record, can the query string be recovered from the page address? The answer did not form a standalone rule at the time, but the practice in the incident was to mark it as missing the first hop and not backfill it from the final address. This question is unrelated to the charset branch and must not be merged into it just because the page is also garbled.

The meeting also included the claim that “English already works correctly, so chunked reading is not a problem.” Multibyte counterexamples later limited that claim: English only covered input that did not cross character boundaries. The claim is still retained as part of the meeting record, but it cannot be included in the current stopping conditions.

## Side issues still unresolved

Whether the URL value used by the test helper code is the same value compared on the routing side cannot be answered by the existing paths and old investigation records. A test that reproduces the result of an input only establishes the relationship between the test input and the observed behavior; the file location does not establish that the production entry point uses the same comparison value.

There are also no new output excerpts supporting whether the reading layer merges chunks before passing them to the decoder, or whether it retains incomplete bytes from the previous chunk when an error occurs. If later records add these two details, preserve this page’s original chunk boundaries rather than pasting only the corrected complete string.

Character set detection, response header rewriting, and page resource rewriting affect the final display, but the existing material does not establish a complete troubleshooting path here. When these symptoms occur together in the live environment, first save the response headers, raw body, and page output separately, then move to the relevant material. Do not assume they belong to the same failure point just because they all appear on the same page.

## Appendix of old examples: notes still visible

### Appendix A: Directory-style URLs

Old note:

> If the URL does not end with `/`, add it first; append the parameters after it. Count it as a pass if the page opens.

This note is outdated. It does not record the first-hop status or state whether the query string changed; “the page opens” cannot replace verification of the replay target. It is retained because an on-call search may still find this text first.

### Appendix B: Decoding by chunk

Old note:

> Run decode whenever a chunk is read, then continue with the next chunk. The English sample works correctly.

This passage only represents the experimental approach used at the time. The English sample did not cover multibyte boundaries, so it cannot be used to judge other content. When citing this note again, add at least the actual chunk boundaries and the complete raw response; without these values, leave it unconfirmed.

### Appendix C: File-related side issue

Under `pywb/rewrite/test/test_wburl.py`, there is still an empty follow-up entry for an adjacent object. The existing material does not explain whether it is connected to trailing-slash normalization or decoding boundaries, so do not move it yet or enter a function name here. The file path can still serve as an entry point into old records, but it cannot substitute for the call relationships themselves.

Do not read the three passages in the appendix as part of the current guidance. They represent, respectively, an old guess about path handling, a chunk-by-chunk experimental approach, and an unlocated file-related side issue; they are retained to show where the records once stopped, not to require reuse of the old steps.

## One last look before handoff

The URL branch must at least show the request, captured object, and first-hop target; the decoding branch must at least show the complete response, actual chunk boundaries, and intermediate results. If either set is missing, stop on that branch. The two symptoms may appear on the same page, but the evidence must still be saved separately.

# History of preload Routing and charset Fallback

This record first addresses two closely related issues with different decision points: resource-type routing for HTML preload, and whether to preserve the original bytes when the charset is wrong. Both investigations start at `pywb/rewrite/html_rewriter.py`.

There were two early options. preload could keep using the shared embedded-resource branch, or it could read `as` during the HTML rewrite stage and then dispatch by type. We initially leaned toward the former because it required fewer changes, but worker and font have different downstream uses, so the tentative decision was to dispatch by type instead. The partial results seen so far are that worker goes through `js_` and font through `oe_`; no table entries are being added for other types yet.

For charset, we also compared three approaches: failing strictly, guessing another encoding, and preserving the original bytes. For now, the decision is to preserve the original bytes so an incorrect declaration doesn't turn the input into replacement characters.
