# pywb Quality Signal Console Troubleshooting Tree

This on-call page originally addressed only one symptom: the current entry point stopped at pywb-quality-signal, and the page did not provide the next segment of signals. The old wording linked this symptom directly to archive capture, so whoever took over would investigate archives, response headers, and replay modifiers in that order. Materials retained later show that missing original records, collection not reaching that point, an exit request not being attached, and a gap in permissions ownership can all make the entry point look “stuck” in the same way.

The old branches have not been deleted, because attachments and screenshots still lead people back here; however, they are no longer suitable as a standalone decision sequence. Now, first confirm what you have, then decide whether you can continue. Rerunning first usually replaces the first anomaly with a new run and cannot be treated as recovery of the incident state.

```text
Does the current entry point retain the original record from this run?
├─ No
│  ├─ Only screenshots remain
│  │  └─ Mark the original request as missing; stop at sample not preserved
│  └─ Even the states before and after the failure are missing
│     └─ Export both sets of states first, then determine whether the record can be obtained
└─ Yes
   ├─ Are the collection and execution states consistent?
   │  ├─ No: first verify whether collection/execution is enabled
   │  └─ Yes: compare with the most recent normal sample to find the first difference
   └─ Where is the first difference?
      ├─ Current entry point or environment: handle it within the Signal Console
      ├─ Archive capture: retain the samples and continue checking the response-header boundary
      ├─ Replay modifiers: gather all materials, then hand off to the interface maintainers
      └─ Requires changing user-visible behavior: stop and enter formal review
```

## Preserve the entry point first, rather than explaining it first

At the start, put the current entry point, original input, revision for that run, and first visible state together. A normal sample is not a substitute; it is only used later to find the first difference. If only the final state remains at the scene, do not split it up to fill in the states before and after the failure; it only indicates the last state read later.

Here, the “original record” means the content left by pywb-quality-signal for that run, not screenshots organized later or a new set of states generated by a rerun. A screenshot can show that the entry point was hit at the time, but may not show the order of the request, collection, and execution. It is acceptable to retain screenshots alongside the record, but not to use them to fill in the request.

The old page described additional collection as a recovery action; that description was later narrowed. Additional collection retains materials for the next observation; the request that was not attached the previous time is still not attached. If the person taking over conflates the two from the start, the tree will incorrectly jump from “no sample” to “confirmed archive difference”.

Only screenshots remain from the old incident corresponding to RPLA-004, and the original request corresponding to the exit entry point was not attached. This branch should stop at “original request missing”. It does not indicate that archive capture failed, nor that replay modifiers were executed; the on-call page only needs to retain the fact that the entry point was hit and identify the missing segment.

If the current entry point does not even have the states before and after the failure, first export both sets of states according to RPLA-021. If the original record still cannot be obtained after export, keep the status “sample not preserved”; do not run a new clean sample as a substitute just to make the tree look complete. A new sample can be used for later comparison, but must not be merged with the first failure.

## Collection and execution are not the same signal

Once you have the original record, first check whether the collection and execution states are consistent. The check retained in RPLA-007 is to confirm whether both sides are enabled; when evidence is missing on one side, do not treat an absent signal as zero or move directly to the replay side. First identify whether the inconsistency is in collection or execution. If the current entry point has no materials, the investigation ends here.

Only when both sides are consistent should you compare against the most recent normal sample. Change only one condition in the comparison. The goal is to find the first difference, not to infer a complete chain from average results, directory names, or the final display. The green status of a normal sample can only help locate the difference; it cannot establish the cause for the failed sample.

If the first difference is at the current entry point or in the environment, continue handling it within pywb · Quality Signal Console. Entry-point changes, collection state, and execution state have still not crossed the project interface, so there is no need to send the materials elsewhere just because the word “stuck” is used. The handoff materials must specify exactly what was compared, rather than simply saying “different from the normal sample”.

The old records include one premature retry. After the rerun turned green, the incident was treated as recovered; this was later changed to prioritize retaining the first failed sample and the environmental differences. Environmental differences here are only part of the comparison conditions. They cannot replace a missing request or turn the unrecorded first run into a confirmed result.

## Narrow the scope only after reaching archive capture

When the first difference falls after archive capture, retain the failed and normal samples first, then continue checking the response-header boundary. This branch only indicates where to look next; it does not directly identify the response-header boundary as the cause. The old attachments include cases where someone cleaned up the incident state or immediately handed it off upon seeing this location, losing the first difference that the next person would need most.

If resource release does not appear, record that the signal has not yet reached that point. This is not evidence of a resource problem, nor can it fill in gaps before archive capture. If the original record already stops earlier, return to the sample-not-preserved branch; do not assign both “abnormal resource release” and “missing request” as causes.

The old tree treated all differences after archive capture as items to hand off. That judgment was later changed: if the difference is still within the Signal Console's own collection, execution, or resource scope, the on-call person continues; prepare a handoff to the corresponding maintainers only when the materials clearly cross the interface. This is not intended to delay handoff, but to avoid sending out a sample with an incomplete entry point only to have it returned.

If the difference already points to replay modifiers, the handoff materials must include at least the original input, revision for that run, failed sample, normal sample, and first difference. If any one of these is missing, return to the earlier preservation branch. Replacing these materials with “it may be replay” neither narrows the problem nor allows the person taking over to check it again.

## Exit actions and gaps in permissions ownership follow separate branches

When an exit action appears but the original request is not attached, still handle it as a screenshot-only incident. It can remain alongside the current entry point, but must not automatically be merged into archive capture. This distinction was unclear in early versions, and some people treated records on the exit side as a confirmed execution chain; now they are treated only as an indication that the original request is missing.

A vacancy in permissions maintenance is another stopping point. RPLA-014 require the temporary person taking over to handle only actions that are due, not define long-term meaning on behalf of pywb · Quality Signal Console. If a permissions issue has already blocked export or reading, state whether the blockage occurred at the entry point, during collection, or before sample comparison; do not merge the gap in permissions ownership and replay modifiers into one branch.

Both issues may exist at the same time: someone lacks permission to export the states before and after the failure, while the record happens to contain a difference near the replay modifiers. In that case, first state which segment of materials cannot be obtained because of permissions. Materials that have not been exported do not become evidence ready for handoff merely because another clue exists.

When user-visible behavior needs to change, the on-call page does not make the decision. Stop at the interface boundary and follow a separate formal review process. What is retained here is the material available at handoff and the material not obtained; do not prewrite conclusions for later decisions.

## Do not fill in the second result retroactively

RPLA-024 retain a case where the result of the second revision was missing. When only the final state remains, keep the second result blank; do not copy the final state into the second result, and do not delete the first failed sample just because recovery occurred later. When both records exist, they can be compared side by side, but still change only one condition.

The absence of a second result does not require the tree to keep simulating a conclusion. The most useful handoff note here is “second result not obtained”, along with the node reached by the first record. Early pages tended to write “may have recovered” here. That judgment has no support from the original record; it is now retained as an old habit and is no longer used as an exit from the tree.

## What to bring when taking over

The project's on-call person receives: the current entry point, whether the original record exists, whether collection and execution are consistent, and the location of the first difference. The interface maintainers receive: the original input, revision for that run, and the first difference between the failed and normal samples. # Caller Integration Maintainer Map

This file keeps the contact map from the caller integration phase, not the full responsibility matrix for sample archive. The earliest table had only three slots: response header boundary, resource release, and preservation worker. That format gave on-call staff somewhere to route a sample, but put “someone is handling the case” and “someone owns the judgment long-term” in the same column. When old samples were reviewed later, empty slots were often misread as default ownership.

The old table is retained below as it was written at the time:

| Old object name | Old entry | What it can still be used for |
|---|---|---|
| `response header boundary` | Module on-call | Route the observation to the module intake point; this does not mean a long-term owner has been confirmed |
| `resource release` | Not yet confirmed | Leave the slot empty until there is an explicit handoff record |
| `preservation worker` | Caller to add a name | Ask the side still using the sample for contact information |

“Module on-call” used to be written as though it meant the person responsible for archive capture. It can now only be understood as a temporary intake point: when there is nowhere else to send a sample, this intake point accepts it first. Whether it then falls within the module's maintenance scope is still for the module maintainer to decide. `resource release` has not gained a name just because the table was filled in. When an old record lacks the intervening handoff, leaving the slot empty is more useful than adding someone who looks plausible.

The three types of action are now recorded separately. sample-archive-client-integration handles intake of integration cases; a temporary handoff only says who is saving materials, following up, or passing them on within a given window; an exit action records what the caller leaves behind after stopping integration. The same sample can trigger all three types of action, but they cannot be combined into one answer to “who is responsible.”

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S[Caller sample] --> I[Project on-call intake]
    I --> Q{Which stage is the issue stuck at}
    Q -->|Integration path or sample record| I
    Q -->|Archive capture or artifacts| M[Module maintainer]
    Q -->|Scope of replay modifiers| D[Relevant decision-maker]
    I --> T[Temporary handoff record]
    I --> E[Exit action record]
    T -.is not equivalent to.-> O[Long-term maintenance relationship]
    E -.preserves.-> R[Last observation]
```

| Item | Recipient | Materials retained at handoff | Where handling stops |
|---|---|---|---|
| Integration feedback from a new caller | sample archive · caller integration on-call | Sample used, integration location, first visible result | Determine whether further assignment is needed |
| Path differences between adjacent revisions | Project on-call | First path difference between the two | Do not directly compare the results of the two runs side by side |
| Archive capture anomalies or artifact differences | Module maintainer | Sample, archive-side observations, existing artifacts | The module decides whether to include it in its maintenance scope |
| Permission, risk, or scope of replay modifiers | Relevant decision-maker | Where the modifier appears and its impact on the caller | The project intake point does not make the technical decision |
| Temporary handoff action | Project on-call | Scope of the handoff, temporary storage location, end condition | Remove the temporary contact when it ends |
| Caller exit | Project on-call | Reason for exit, sample retention location, last observation | Do not supply a technical conclusion for resource release |
| `resource release` | Empty slot | Known case details and previous contacts | Wait for an explicit handoff to a specialist maintainer |
| Contact information for `preservation worker` | Caller to provide | Sample still in use or a confirmed window | Keep it empty until supplied |

The role of RPLB-001 is narrowly scoped. It requires starting from an adjacent revision with a working path and comparing only the first path difference. This comparison can help the on-call person decide whether the sample needs to go to the module maintainer, but it cannot prove that the archive side has changed. A later review also pointed out that the original input and the present result may not belong to the same run. When old links, old screenshots, and results obtained later are put together, label them separately first, then decide whether to keep looking for a contact.

Revalidation in the shared environment still uses the original sample-archive-client-integration entry point indicated by RPLB-006. Local samples are only material for locating the issue; they cannot replace observations in the shared environment. RPLB-009 continues to look for the last teams still using adj-sample-archive. Even if the search ultimately finds that no one is using it, that only affects whether new samples can be obtained; it does not make the project on-call person the long-term owner.

RPLB-014 corresponds to missing intervening records. The old approach used here remains to leave the slot blank: if there are no handoff materials between two records, do not invent a handoff relationship from their chronological order. RPLB-017 is used to check the old entry point, the present target, and the last person to confirm it. Slots left by people who have left the company remain empty. This makes aggregation inconvenient, but prevents an old entry point from being misrepresented as still having a long-term maintainer.

Exit actions and resource release also used to be grouped together. That section no longer applies, but it is retained because old links still bring people here. Exit records need to retain the sample and the last observation; resource release requires an explicit specialist maintenance relationship. The two may happen within the same window, but cannot substitute for each other. The same applies to temporary handoffs: someone having handled it does not mean someone owns it long-term.

One line is enough when taking over: who accepted the integration sample, where the materials are temporarily stored, whether they have been passed to the module maintainer or the relevant decision-maker, and whether the caller exited or was still using it at the end. If the long-term owner has not been confirmed, leave the last item blank. Navigation still starts from `docs/adj-sample-archive/ownership/sample-archive-client-integration-current maintainer map.md`; the body and attachments under that path are maintained by sample archive · caller integration, so the old entry-point name is also retained.

The processing sequence in RPLC-005 preserved the baseline before starting cleanup; after the old index was cleared, the execution record could still be opened from historical records. The window-closing record therefore needs to document the page entry point and the execution record's destination separately, rather than combining them into a single “available” state.

RPLC-009 left another easily confused state: there is a record for the person on duty, but the execution record still points to an old repository or source. The handoff location can help locate the record, but cannot supply missing run results for the current entry point. If the execution record points to an old source, keep its destination and this window's entry point location, then stop at the verification step; do not label the old source as the current revision just because someone took over.

Even if the entry page and the execution record appear to have the same content, check both destinations. The same title, the same page excerpt, and even historical records opening normally are not enough to prove that the record comes from this window. This distinction is precisely what is most easily lost after the entry point is replaced or the old index is cleaned up.

## Record output fields in the order events occurred

Preserve at least the last actual output from the window exactly as it was. Record zero output as well; do not change it to success because the page is green. Split the record into three fields: input or version, first output, and second output. In each field, specify whether it came from the current entry point, the original current revision, or the page after temporary diagnostics.

- [ ] In the input field, write the input or revision visible at the start of the window; leave it blank if missing.
- [ ] The first output should contain only what the first actual run or read produced; do not replace it with a later page state.
- [ ] Keep the second output separately. If there was no second run or read, state the gap explicitly; do not copy the first field.
- [ ] If `Archive capture` left only a status with no corresponding artifact, mark the status field as unconfirmed.

RPLC-014 recorded a case where the second result for the current revision was missing and only the final state remained. In this case, retain only the fact that “the second run or read is missing”; do not copy the first result or change the blank to “no impact”. If the first field is also missing, do not fill it back in with a value that appeared on the page later; fill the corresponding position only after obtaining the original input or run record again.

RPLC-001 also exposed a mismatch between the current revision and the page chronology. In this type of case, reorder the existing records by their original times, using the page's final value only as corroborating evidence. Do not move the final value into the first result, and do not overwrite the original records already left in the window with an order reconstructed later. Reordering only helps clarify the sequence; it does not supply missing input, second output, or archive artifacts.

If temporary diagnostics change the page or entry point, prioritize saving the output from before the change and keep the post-change result separately; do not combine the two into a single run record. If the result cannot be matched to the entry point, retain the original output and the entry point location, and stop at the recording stage for now. The page turning green again does not erase the distinction between before and after diagnostics.

## Keep borrowed items separate from page cleanup

This table records only items borrowed during this window that need to be returned; do not expand it into a full resource inventory for the documentation site. Write “still in use”, “returned”, or “return status unknown” beside each item; add the return time when it can be confirmed. Borrowed items with unclear purposes cannot simply be marked as returned either, because it is impossible to determine whether they still support the current entry point or the last read.

- [ ] Check each borrowed item, its purpose, and its return status against the checklist from the start of the window.
- [ ] Do not simply cross out items that were returned but have no return time; keep them pending confirmation.
- [ ] If an item is still in use or its return status is unknown, do not withdraw temporary content related to it.
- [ ] Use handoff records only to locate the actual handoff location; do not fabricate return records for each unresolved item.
- [ ] If returning an item would prevent further evidence collection through the current entry point, first save the last output and the entry point location, then pause the return.

The handoff information in RPLC-005 also includes this: groups that have already gone offline should be removed from the new entry point. This action targets only the old handoff locations on the entry point; it does not mean rewriting the maintenance relationships for the entire documentation site. If an old location has been removed but a borrowed item has no return record, still treat its return status as unknown; do not assume that the borrowing of items left by a group has ended just because that group no longer appears on the entry point.

The confirmed handoff in RPLC-009 does not change this judgment. Handoff confirmation means someone has taken over the location; it does not mean the last output has been completed, nor does it mean the original current revision is readable. What must be retained at the end of the window is the known return status and unconfirmed items, rather than replacing them with handoff status.

## Stop points before withdrawal

Before withdrawal, reopen the current entry point and confirm that the target is indeed temporary content left by this window. Do not consider the withdrawal target confirmed just because a historical page, cached page, or index page can still display the content. Matching page titles are not enough either; at a minimum, the entry point location, current revision, and window records must match.

1. [ ] Save the entry point location, current revision, last output, and borrowed-item status.
2. [ ] Check the destinations of the current entry point and execution record; if they differ, stop and do not withdraw.
3. [ ] Confirm that the artifact or status of `Archive capture` has been retained as it actually was; if the artifact is missing, do not use the status as evidence of completion.
4. [ ] Open the withdrawal entry point, confirm that the objects listed there belong to this window, then perform one withdrawal.
5. [ ] After withdrawal, re-enter through the current entry point and confirm that the temporary content can no longer be retrieved.
6. [ ] Stop further cleanup if the current entry point can still retrieve the temporary content, the withdrawal entry point disappears, it redirects to an old source, or the results seen on rechecking cannot be matched to the pre-withdrawal records.

Withdrawal handles only confirmed temporary content. Do not tidy up the release notes along the way, do not treat the old index as a withdrawal target, and do not expand the withdrawal scope because the handoff location has changed. If the entry point redirects to an old location, first retain the redirected address and the pre-withdrawal page; do not continue trying. Also stop if the execution record still points to an old source; that is a problem with the record's destination and cannot be corrected by another withdrawal.

If the current entry point can no longer retrieve the temporary content after withdrawal, record only the result corresponding to that action; do not attribute all other page changes to the withdrawal. If the temporary content can still be retrieved after withdrawal, retain the entry point and page as they were at that time, and stop the next cleanup step. Do not try to fill in recovery steps without recovery records for the shared environment.

## Retain the earlier stop points

The early checklist used only “do not clear the state after seeing the mount prefix” as a stop point. This state marker is still retained, but it can only serve as a reminder to preserve things first; it cannot replace checks of the entry point, revision, output, and execution record. If `Compatibility window` cannot be found, stop at the current record; finding it does not mean input and output preservation can be skipped.

`Client proxy` and `Mount prefix` remain page clues that can be recorded when locating the entry point. They do not indicate that the old index has been fully cleared, nor that the execution record has switched to the current source. These clues are used only to place the page seen during the window alongside the last output; they cannot independently justify withdrawal.

The page chronology issue in RPLC-001, the old-source record in RPLC-009, and the missing second result in RPLC-014 should each remain in their respective fields. The first addresses ordering, the second addresses the record's destination, and the third preserves the output gap. Compressing them into a single statement that “the page has a problem” would lose the stop points that actually need to be assessed when closing the window.

After the window ends, it is sufficient to retain the current entry point location, last output, return status of borrowed items, and withdrawal entry point results. Write whether historical records still open and why an old repository or source still appears beside the execution record's destination; do not bring the documentation site's entire index history into the window-closing checklist. There are still no shared-environment records for recovery actions after withdrawal; if withdrawal fails, retain only the entry point and page seen at the time of failure, and do not add a set of recovery steps here.

# Documentation Site Cache and State Trade-offs

The issue at the time was not the page content itself, but how to preserve the state of tests disabled · User Documentation Site / tests-disabled-documentation-portal. There were two options: continue examining the cache through the `preservation worker`, or split out the `regression samples` and then rebuild an environment. Both would produce readable material, but they would preserve different relationships between pages.

The decision was to retain the `current revision` first and not rebuild the environment. Pages, attachments, and pre-change routes would stay where they were, so their relationships at the time would remain visible during later review. The `regression samples` would be handled as a separate follow-up, not folded into this preservation effort. The trade-off here was to preserve the original state, not to claim that the samples had already been split out or that a new set of validation results existed.

Those in favor of splitting out the samples were concerned that continuing to handle the cache through the `preservation worker` would mix old content with new observations. That concern was valid: if the environment were reorganized first, a failure would be hard to attribute to either the cache trade-off or the content after the pages were recombined. But reorganization itself would change the input. Rebuilt pages could not replace the current revision or be used to overwrite the original attachment and route relationships.

The sequence was therefore set: preserve the state first, then handle the samples. If the `regression samples` do need to be split out later, that must be written up as a new record; results from the new environment must not be backfilled into this decision. The list of active callers for `rollback observation` was incomplete at the time. Whether rollback should restore only the old entry point was also not settled by this decision. These two gaps did not affect retaining the current revision, but they would affect how to exit later.

A later exit action found that routes to the old `exit action` still remained. The resolution was to delete the entry points pointing to the old action while retaining a snapshot of the pre-change routes. This cleaned up the entry points; it did not rebuild the environment or change the current revision that had already been retained. The related state can be reviewed in `docs/adj-tests-disabled/decisions/tests-disabled-documentation-portal-Cache and Original State Trade-offs.md`; DOC-40 contain adjacent records.

# Decision for this archive maintenance window

We compared two options during the maintenance window: keep the existing resource-lifecycle entry point, or use the window to adjust the entry point and move the related checks along with it. The tentative choice is the former.

This is not because the entry point cannot be changed. The evidence available for this round only covers the results for the same archive input on the server, in the page runtime, and across the resource lifecycle. Combining an entry point adjustment with these results in a single window would make it impossible to tell where the changes came from in a later review.

For this round, record the actual impact, the coordinator, and the old entry point we can revert to. The coordinator must first save the fallback location for the old entry point. If the existing observations cannot be reproduced, or if any of the observations in the three areas cannot be explained, we will not proceed with a decision to make the adjustment in this window. An entry point adjustment can still be proposed again after the window closes, but it must include reproduction materials for the same archive input.

The objection remains on record: continuing to use the old entry point will delay cleanup and may lead people who come later to mistake it for the long-term home. This conclusion is only a trade-off within the maintenance window; it does not establish the old entry point as a permanent solution.

# Archive Maintenance Window Decision for This Round

This record preserves the trade-offs made during a maintenance window, not the current description of the resource lifecycle. The draft reduced the issue to “do not change the entry point for now,” but a later review found that this wording easily conflated two different judgments: first, whether the window could accommodate an entry-point adjustment; and second, whether the existing observations could support a broader compatibility conclusion. Neither was completely ruled out at the time, but neither should have been written as completed.

The window discussion always concerned the same archived input. The judgment was not based on whether an individual local call appeared to work normally; it required looking at the observable results on the server side, in the page runtime, and across the resource lifecycle at the same time. This constraint was intended to prevent treating the page's behavior as evidence that the server side was already stable, and to prevent mistaking local phenomena related to resource release for general results in the page runtime. The draft did not clearly state this distinction and only left the conclusion to “keep the current entry point”; therefore, the old wording is retained below and must not be cited on its own.

> Draft conclusion (original intent preserved): During the maintenance window, first keep the current resource-lifecycle entry point. Do not advance the adjustment window in parallel with entry-point migration. The coordinator preserves the rollback location for the old entry point; if the review cannot explain any observation, roll back the adjustment.

After review, the decision was not changed to “the entry point must never change.” Instead, it became a narrower window decision: this round approves only the scope covered by the existing evidence. The existing materials support comparing the results in three places using the same archived input; anything not supported by the materials is not automatically included just because the maintenance window has already been scheduled. The resource-lifecycle entry point remains in place so that this comparison has a stable reference point, not as a judgment that the entry point belongs there permanently.

## The two approaches considered at the time

The first approach was to keep the current resource-lifecycle entry point and use the window to collect and review the existing observations. Its cost was straightforward: the old entry point would remain in the everyday lookup path, and people organizing things later would still have to determine which descriptions applied only to this window. Its benefit was equally clear: the server side, page runtime, and resource lifecycle could continue to be compared around the same archived input; if the results differed, the discrepancy itself could be addressed first instead of first suspecting that entry-point migration had introduced a new variable.

The second approach was to adjust the entry point during the window while also moving the existing descriptions, call relationships, and lookup locations into the new arrangement. The people who proposed this approach were concerned that the old entry point would continue accumulating supplementary descriptions, and that a maintenance window was one of the few periods suitable for centralized cleanup. The objection was not that cleanup had no value, but that the materials available at the time were insufficient to separate “the result after the entry point was adjusted” from “the result of the archived input itself.” If both things happened at once, then even if a later review found that the page-runtime and resource-lifecycle observations were inconsistent, it would be difficult to determine which part should be rolled back.

A compromise of “migrate half first” was not adopted at the time. On the surface, this arrangement preserved an escape route, but in practice it would create two places that could be treated as entry points: the old entry point would still handle some lookups, while the new entry point would handle some maintenance. For this window, a partial migration would make it impossible for the coordinator to clearly record which part could be rolled back, and would not tell reviewers which path to use to compare the same archived input again. Therefore, the decision was not to break the adjustment into smaller pieces, but to defer it until independent supporting materials were available.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Same archived input] --> B[Server-side result]
    A --> C[Page-runtime result]
    A --> D[Resource-lifecycle result]
    B --> E{Can the existing materials be matched}
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E -->|Can be matched| F[Record only the covered scope]
    E -->|Cannot be matched| G[Keep the old entry point and roll back the adjustment]
```

“Can be matched” in the diagram does not require the three results to be exactly the same. The server side, page runtime, and resource lifecycle are different locations by nature; what is recorded is whether they can be explained by the same archived input, and whether the change in the window causes that explanation to drift. The draft expressed this as “do not proceed if any one part cannot be explained.” The meaning was not wrong, but it lacked a comparison subject. The restriction added during review was that scattered results from different archived inputs cannot be assembled into a single passing judgment, and the approval scope cannot be expanded based only on normal behavior in one location.

## Decision made

During the maintenance window, keep the current resource-lifecycle entry point and remove the entry-point adjustment from this round's decision. The window may still handle maintenance matters adjacent to that entry point, but any action that changes the lookup location, explanation path, or availability of the old entry point is not considered approved for this round. This is not because the entry-point adjustment was proven problematic; at the time, there simply was not enough material to prove that it could safely be included in the same batch of changes as the existing observations.

The decision also requires three types of window records to be retained. The first is actual impact: what observable results the same archived input produced on the server side, in the page runtime, and across the resource lifecycle; which results were merely local phenomena; and which could be matched to one another. The second is coordination information: someone is responsible for keeping the comparison materials, the reason for not adjusting yet, and the rollback location together, so that the window does not end with only the statement “we did not change it at the time.” The third is a rollback-capable old entry point: the old entry point must remain usable for review until the later adjustment has its own comparison materials. The coordinator here is a window responsibility, not a reassignment of the long-term ownership of any component.

“Rollback-capable” also had a deliberately narrowed meaning at the time. It does not promise to retain every old description, nor does it require working from the old entry point forever; it only requires that, if a later finding shows the judgment to be invalid, it must still be possible to return to the location on which this comparison depended and review the results of the same archived input in the three places again. If the old entry point were cleaned up first and it were discovered only later that the page-runtime conclusion could not be matched to the resource lifecycle, the decision left by the maintenance window would lose its point of verification. Therefore, keep the entry point first and schedule the adjustment afterward.

## Extensions not approved

The meeting materials proposed framing the maintenance window as a broader compatibility closeout. This proposal was not adopted. The reason was not that compatibility was unimportant, but that the materials for this round were sufficient only for the scope covered by the existing evidence. Including a broader judgment in the decision would make readers think that situations beyond the server side, page runtime, and resource lifecycle had already been compared; in reality, unconfirmed areas should remain unconfirmed.

“Nothing abnormal was observed in the page runtime” was also not treated as a reason to continue. This wording was tempting in the earlier discussion because it could make the window appear to have a positive signal already; however, it cannot replace the correspondence among the three sets of results. Conversely, if the resource-lifecycle observations still require additional assumptions to explain, local stability in the page runtime cannot endorse the entry-point adjustment. This cautious wording was retained after review to prevent people later from reading a single-point result as an overall result.

Another option that was not adopted was to move all reservations to a later document and leave only a brief decision here. That would make the decision appear cleaner, but would erase the reasons for opposing the entry-point adjustment at the time. The reservations include the following: keeping the old entry point would increase cleanup costs; the evidence within the window was uneven; and adjusting the entry point could conceal interpretive differences that already existed. These reservations are not action items for the next round, but background on why the two things were not combined this round.

## Review addendum

The review did not add a conclusion covering every situation; instead, it separated the overly simplified wording in the draft. The current record should be read as follows: the window decided to keep the old entry point, the approval scope is limited to the existing evidence, and unconfirmed areas do not become confirmed merely because the window has ended. The draft's wording “tentatively choose the former” still describes the direction taken at the time, but interpreting it as a long-term architectural decision would exceed its original intent.

The resource-lifecycle entry point remains a lookup point during this period, not the only technical explanation. The server-side results and page-runtime results are equally part of the comparison; if a later adjustment updates the description in only one of these places, it cannot inherit the judgment in this decision. If a window adjustment is proposed again later, it should separately state what the adjustment will change and include comparison materials for the same archived input, rather than citing “the old entry point was retained previously” as automatic permission.

DOC-44 records the handoff for the browser-matrix rotation. The two materials can link to each other, but the browser rotation does not replace the entry-point judgment here; this page also makes no decision about the browser matrix. They are kept separate because one addresses the trade-offs within a maintenance window, while the other addresses the arrangement for the handoff.

The parts that remain unconfirmed are retained as follows: whether the existing observations cover all maintenance actions adjacent to the old entry point; how the comparison materials should be grouped if the entry-point adjustment inevitably occurs at the same time as other window changes; and how long the old entry point should be retained during subsequent cleanup. These questions received no new answers in this review, so they should not be rewritten as conditions that have already been decided.

Finally, one old judgment that is no longer fully accurate but remains useful is retained: the draft treated “keeping the entry point” as the primary risk-reduction action. After review, a more accurate formulation is that confusion is reduced by fixing the comparison subject as the same archived input and limiting the approval scope to areas covered by existing evidence; keeping the entry point merely makes this limitation reviewable. The old sentence is not deleted because it explains why the retention path was chosen first at the time.

# cookie-state Dependency Freeze Entry Point Notes

This investigation starts with a state name, but its only concrete anchor is a test location in the repository. First find the `cookie` matches in `tests_disabled/test_proxy_https_cookie.py`, then inspect where the state at each hit enters and which direct call site it is passed to. Don't treat “dependency upgrade freeze” as a directory name up front, and don't combine files into one chain just because several of them contain cookie.

At this point, only this segment can be documented:

```text
cookie-state
    |
    v
 tests_disabled/test_proxy_https_cookie.py
    |
    v
 A direct usage point
    |
    v
 The first actual consumer of the dependency upgrade freeze
```

## Start at the hit location

`tests_disabled/test_proxy_https_cookie.py` serves only to locate the code. When reading the `cookie` hit, also inspect the nearby inputs, outputs, and state propagation; don't read the entire test directory as a single module. What needs to be confirmed is what shape cookie-state takes in this test, and whether the test passes the state into the call or compares the call result.

These two possibilities change the next step. If the state is test input, the direct call site is the entry point of the system under test, so follow the called object. If the state appears in an assertion or result, first trace back to the object that produced the state, then determine whether the call site actually passes it into the next layer. The file hit alone cannot determine the direction; where the state enters or leaves is the branch point in this local path.

Other `cookie` text in the test file does not automatically become part of the path. It may be a fixture, a comparison value, or an adjacent test scenario. This record keeps only one direct usage point that can be reached from the hit; there is no need to stitch multiple test scenarios into a seemingly complete call chain just to cover results with the same name.

## Follow only one call edge

After reaching the direct call site, the next stop is only the object actually called there. Earlier notes treated the “call name” as a direction hint, not as an ownership determination. If the call site can pass the state to the next layer, continue to see how that layer first uses it. If the call site only receives and compares the result, record it first as an observation point; don't write the test assertion up as the implementation location of the freeze item.

Files with the same name, tests with the same name, and adjacent directories only show that the search results are close to one another. If they have no call edge leading out from the current usage point, they remain signposts. In particular, don't place another file after the direct call site just because it also contains `cookie`; that would mistake search order for a program relationship.

On this page, “first actual consumer” means the object where the dependency upgrade freeze result is first used. The file where the keyword appears earliest is not necessarily the consumer, and the test that exposes the problem is not necessarily the consumer either. After following the direct call, look for the location where the result is first actually read or used. No function name can currently be publicly confirmed, so this description continues to use “first actual consumer.”

## Where to place the packet capture

The replay packet capture is locating material alongside the code path. It can be used to check the shape of cookie-state appearing on this path—for example, whether the state still appears with the same replay request, or whether the value seen in the test can be matched to a corresponding position in the request data. The packet capture only helps identify the object; it does not replace the call edge in the repository.

A matching field name in the packet capture cannot add a new entry point. The order in which things appear in the packet capture also cannot be used to infer module call order; the direct usage point in the code remains the basis for the next stop. If the state in the packet capture cannot be matched to the test hit, stop at the current call site, record the inconsistency, and then confirm whether the test input and replay request refer to the same path.

This is also why “dependency upgrade freeze” should not be located by working backward from the packet capture. The packet capture can show what a replay request carried, but not which file owns the freeze result. Directory ownership and the consumption location must be confirmed through repository call relationships, not filled in from field names or request order.

## Stop points to preserve at handoff

The actual trace can be split into three local actions. First, inspect only the inputs, outputs, and state propagation around the `cookie` hit in `tests_disabled/test_proxy_https_cookie.py`; don't scan all cookie files at once. Second, follow one direct call site to the next layer and record the object it actually consumes. Third, use the replay packet capture for a local comparison. If the comparison cannot be matched to a code location, return to the current call site and do not extend the chain downward.

When the path reaches a point that requires the owner familiar with “dependency upgrade freeze” to explain it, stop there. This does not assign an unconfirmed name to the first consumer or expand the test directory into the maintenance boundary of the freeze item. title: Postmortem: Replay On-Call Handoff Discrepancy

versions.body:
# Postmortem: Replay On-Call Handoff Discrepancy

This discrepancy occurred during a replay on-call handoff window. The incoming shift had already started observing according to the original plan when they found that the results seen by the browser probe did not match that plan. The team did not record this as a failure of the entire replay service; all they could confirm was that one visible result during the handoff had deviated from expectations. That distinction affected both the recovery approach and the subsequent decision not to withdraw the old entry point immediately.

## What Happened During the Shift

- Before the handoff began, the original plan was still being followed within the established window. No exception had been called out for the browser probe, and no alternative observation entry point had been prepared.
- After the handoff started, the browser probe returned results inconsistent with the handoff expectations. The initial description called it only a “discrepancy within the window,” without attributing the visible behavior directly to any part of the replay path.
- After the difference was found, the coordinator kept the old entry point in place, with the option to withdraw it. Temporary recovery first allowed the handoff to continue; the recovery action was not treated as confirmation of the cause.
- The restored entry point was used for continued observation. The probe was not treated as complete diagnostic evidence. It was retained along with the other incident material to help determine later whether the discrepancy lay in observation, the entry point, or the replay results.

The actual impact on the shift was narrow: on-call staff could no longer use the visible results from the original plan as the basis for the handoff and had to observe through the temporarily restored entry point instead. There was no record of the number of requests affected, the duration of the impact, or the range of affected pages, so this window cannot establish that all replay requests had the same discrepancy. The coordinator was responsible for retaining the old entry point and continued to control when to withdraw it after recovery. This let the next shift see both the pre-recovery and post-recovery observation points, rather than receiving only a fully replaced result.

## Earlier Assessment Retained

The initial draft provisionally classified the issue as a presentation discrepancy during the handoff window and, based on the results after temporary recovery, assumed that replay itself had not changed. That assessment is retained here to explain why the shift did not stop the entire handoff. It is not a root-cause conclusion: the browser probe can show only what was visible on screen at the time. It cannot prove which component caused the discrepancy or that the original plan would have produced the same results through other entry points.

The temporary recovery worked, but that establishes only that the handoff could continue. It may have changed the observation entry point, bypassed the difference in the original plan, or simply stopped the probe from showing the same symptom; the incident material could not distinguish among these possibilities. The recovery time therefore cannot be read as the time the issue was localized. The old entry point was not deleted immediately after recovery precisely to avoid erasing this still-unresolved difference along with it.

## Questions Left Open in the Window

- At what stage did the browser probe and the original plan start producing different results;
- Whether temporary recovery changed the entry point, the probe's observations, or the replay results themselves;
- Whether enough material would remain after the old entry point was withdrawn to reexamine the differences within this window;
- Whether the discrepancy seen by the incoming shift was specific to this window, or whether the original plan already had undocumented conditions.

This record captures only the sequence of initial discovery, temporary recovery, and handling of the old entry point. When reviewing it later, distinguish “the handoff was restored” from “the discrepancy was localized”; the former was established during the shift, while the latter was still unknown at the time.
